Few areas of biomedicine have generated as much public expectation as stem cell research, owing to the capacity of certain cells to differentiate into a wide range of specialised tissues and thereby, in principle, to repair organs damaged by injury or degenerative disease. The translation of this potential into approved treatments, however, has proved considerably slower than early enthusiasts predicted. At present, only a limited number of stem cell-based therapies, most notably bone marrow transplantation for certain blood disorders, are regarded as established medical practice. For the majority of other conditions, the evidence of safety and efficacy remains at the stage of early clinical trials.
This gap between expectation and evidence has been exploited by a growing number of private clinics in several countries, which market unproven stem cell injections directly to patients for conditions ranging from arthritis to multiple sclerosis. Such interventions are frequently administered without the controlled trials that regulatory agencies normally require. Moreover, a number of serious adverse events, including infections, tumour formation and loss of vision, have been documented in the medical literature. Patients, many of whom suffer from conditions for which conventional medicine offers little hope, may pay substantial sums for procedures whose benefits have never been demonstrated.
Regulators have responded in divergent ways. Some agencies have tightened their oversight, insisting that products involving substantial manipulation of cells be evaluated as medicines, while others have introduced accelerated approval pathways intended to speed patient access to promising therapies. Critics of the latter approach contend that lowering the evidential threshold risks legitimising treatments before their effectiveness has been established, whereas its supporters maintain that excessively rigid rules may deprive seriously ill patients of their only realistic options.

questions.passage:
It has become commonplace to attribute the apparent intensification of political polarisation in many democracies to the spread of social media, whose recommendation algorithms are said to confine users within so-called echo chambers in which they encounter only opinions that confirm their existing beliefs. Although intuitively persuasive, this account has received only partial support from empirical research. Large-scale analyses of online behaviour indicate that most users are in fact exposed to a more diverse range of news sources than the echo chamber hypothesis would predict. Strongly segregated information diets, by contrast, appear to be characteristic mainly of a relatively small, highly engaged minority.
Moreover, the chronology of polarisation complicates any simple causal explanation. In the United States, for instance, the divergence between the major parties was already well under way before the emergence of social networking platforms. Some studies have even reported that polarisation increased most rapidly among older citizens, the demographic group least likely to use such platforms. Experimental evidence is similarly mixed: in several studies, participants who temporarily deactivated their accounts reported modest reductions in hostility towards political opponents, whereas other experiments found that exposure to opposing views actually strengthened, rather than moderated, the original positions of participants.
None of this implies that social media are irrelevant. A more plausible interpretation, according to a number of political scientists, is that digital platforms amplify tendencies rooted in longer-term developments, such as the reorganisation of party coalitions, the fragmentation of traditional broadcasting and growing economic inequality. On this view, the principal effect of social media may be less to create divisions than to make existing ones more visible and emotionally charged, a distinction with considerable consequences for the design of effective policy responses.

questions.passage:
Along temperate coastlines, where mangroves cannot survive, salt marshes perform many of the same ecological functions. These grassy wetlands, which are flooded and drained by the tides twice a day, provide nursery grounds for fish, feeding areas for migrating birds and a natural buffer that absorbs the energy of waves during storms. They are also remarkably efficient at storing carbon: because their waterlogged soils contain little oxygen, plant material decomposes very slowly and can accumulate over centuries.
Despite these benefits, salt marshes have long been regarded as wasteland. Over the past few hundred years, large areas in Europe and North America were drained for agriculture, built on or enclosed behind sea walls. The walls themselves have created a further problem known as coastal squeeze. As sea levels rise, marshes would naturally migrate inland, but where a hard barrier blocks their path, they are gradually drowned and disappear.
In recent decades, some coastal authorities have begun to change their approach. Under a policy often described as managed realignment, old sea walls are deliberately breached or moved further inland, allowing the tide to flood former farmland so that new marshes can form. Supporters argue that such schemes can be cheaper in the long run than maintaining ever-higher defences. The policy is not without its difficulties, however. Landowners may be reluctant to give up productive fields, and newly created marshes often take decades to develop the full range of plants and animals found in natural ones. For this reason, many ecologists stress that restoring lost marshes is no substitute for protecting those that still exist.

questions.passage:
Bronze, an alloy made by combining copper with a small amount of tin, was harder than pure copper and could be cast into a wide variety of shapes, from axes and swords to ornaments and vessels. Its adoption, beginning in parts of western Asia around 3000 BC and spreading gradually across Europe and beyond, was so significant that nineteenth-century scholars named an entire period of prehistory after it. Yet the metal posed a puzzle that archaeologists are still working to solve. Copper deposits are fairly common, but tin is rare, and in many regions where bronze was widely used there were no local sources of it at all.
This scarcity meant that bronze production depended on trade networks that often stretched over very long distances. Chemical and isotopic analyses of tin ingots recovered from shipwrecks in the eastern Mediterranean, for example, suggest that some of the metal may have come from as far away as Cornwall in Britain or from deposits in Central Asia. Such findings indicate that communities separated by thousands of kilometres were linked, directly or through many intermediaries, by the exchange of metals.
Some historians argue that this dependence also made Bronze Age societies vulnerable. When trade routes were disrupted, as appears to have happened in the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BC, palaces that controlled the supply of metal could lose much of their wealth and authority. Whether the disruption of the tin trade actually contributed to the collapse of several states at that time remains uncertain, since droughts, earthquakes and invasions have also been proposed as causes. It is notable, however, that iron, whose ores are found almost everywhere, became increasingly common in the centuries that followed.

questions.passage:
Bronze, an alloy made by combining copper with a small amount of tin, was harder than pure copper and could be cast into a wide variety of shapes, from axes and swords to ornaments and vessels. Its adoption, beginning in parts of western Asia around 3000 BC and spreading gradually across Europe and beyond, was so significant that nineteenth-century scholars named an entire period of prehistory after it. Yet the metal posed a puzzle that archaeologists are still working to solve. Copper deposits are fairly common, but tin is rare, and in many regions where bronze was widely used there were no local sources of it at all.
This scarcity meant that bronze production depended on trade networks that often stretched over very long distances. Chemical and isotopic analyses of tin ingots recovered from shipwrecks in the eastern Mediterranean, for example, suggest that some of the metal may have come from as far away as Cornwall in Britain or from deposits in Central Asia. Such findings indicate that communities separated by thousands of kilometres were linked, directly or through many intermediaries, by the exchange of metals.
Some historians argue that this dependence also made Bronze Age societies vulnerable. When trade routes were disrupted, as appears to have happened in the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BC, palaces that controlled the supply of metal could lose much of their wealth and authority. Whether the disruption of the tin trade actually contributed to the collapse of several states at that time remains uncertain, since droughts, earthquakes and invasions have also been proposed as causes. It is notable, however, that iron, whose ores are found almost everywhere, became increasingly common in the centuries that followed.

explain how tin was extracted from its ores
argue that iron caused the droughts and earthquakes of 1200 BC
prove that palaces controlled the supply of iron
suggest that a metal with widely available ores was less dependent on long-distance trade

Demirin bronzdan ‘harder’ olduğu karşılaştırması, kalayın nasıl ‘extracted’ edildiği, demirin kuraklık ve depremlere ‘caused’ olduğu ve sarayların demir arzını ‘controlled’ ettiği metinde yer almaz.

questions.passage: Across a wide range of cultures, adults who address babies tend to change the way they speak in strikingly similar ways. Their pitch rises, their intonation becomes more exaggerated, their sentences grow shorter and they repeat themselves far more often than they would with another adult. For much of the twentieth century, this style of speech, often dismissed as 'baby talk', was regarded by some educators as harmful, on the grounds that it supplied children with a distorted model of the language they were expected to learn. Research over the past few decades has largely reversed this verdict. Infants, it turns out, generally prefer listening to infant-directed speech, and the features that make it sound odd to adult ears may be precisely those that help a child break into language. Exaggerated pitch contours seem to capture and hold attention, while slower, more carefully articulated vowels may make it easier to tell similar sounds apart. Frequent pauses at the boundaries between phrases could, in turn, offer clues to where one word or grammatical unit ends and the next begins. None of this means that infant-directed speech is necessary for language acquisition. In some communities, adults rarely address young children directly, yet those children still become fluent speakers, presumably by listening to the conversations going on around them. What the research does suggest is that the style is not a careless simplification but a form of communication finely tuned to a listener whose abilities are changing month by month. Indeed, parents appear to adjust it as their children grow, moving gradually towards adult-like speech as the child's own vocabulary expands. Whether they make these adjustments consciously, however, remains an open question.
questions.text: The passage is mainly concerned with ----.
options: the reasons why some communities refuse to speak to their children until they can talk
the harmful effects of baby talk on children's later reading skills
the differences between the vocabularies of adults and young children
how views on the way adults speak to babies have changed and why this style of speech may help infants learn language
the methods that teachers use to correct young children's pronunciation
questions.explanation: Parça, yetişkinlerin bebeklerle konuşma biçiminin bir zamanlar zararlı sayıldığını, bugün ise bu konuşmanın dil edinimine yardımcı olabileceğinin düşünüldüğünü anlatır. Bazı toplulukların çocuklarla az konuşması yalnızca bir örnektir ve 'refuse' (reddetmek) fikri parçada yoktur; okuma becerilerine ('reading skills') zarar parçada geçmez; kelime dağarcığı farkları ('vocabularies') ve öğretmenlerin telaffuz düzeltme yöntemleri ('pronunciation') ana konu değildir.

questions.passage: The idea that daily life should be organised around short trips rather than long ones is hardly new, but it has gained remarkable momentum in recent years under the label of the '15-minute city'. Popularised by the urbanist Carlos Moreno, the concept proposes that residents should be able to reach most of what they need, from schools and shops to clinics, parks and workplaces, within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. Its appeal is easy to understand. Shorter journeys mean less traffic, cleaner air and more time for family and leisure, while busier local streets may support small businesses and strengthen a sense of community. Paris made the idea a central part of its planning agenda, converting parking spaces into cycle lanes and opening some school playgrounds to the public outside school hours. Barcelona's 'superblocks', in which groups of city blocks are closed to through traffic and their inner streets given over to pedestrians, are often cited as a related experiment. Yet the concept has also attracted criticism from several directions. Some planners note that it suits dense European cities far better than sprawling ones, where the population within a fifteen-minute radius may be too small to sustain a hospital or a secondary school. Others warn that improving a neighbourhood's amenities can push up property prices and gradually displace the very residents it was meant to serve. A third objection concerns employment: few people are free to choose a job simply because it is close to home. Supporters reply that the 15-minute city was never intended as a rigid rule but as a direction of travel, a way of asking which services could reasonably be brought closer to the people who use them.
questions.text: According to the passage, the 15-minute city concept ----.
options: aims to put most everyday services within a short walk or bicycle ride of people's homes
requires every resident to work within fifteen minutes of home
was first put into practice in Barcelona's superblocks
is mainly intended to bring down property prices in city centres
has been rejected by planners working in dense European cities
questions.explanation: Parçaya göre kavram, okul, dükkân, klinik, park ve iş yerleri gibi ihtiyaçların yürüyerek ya da bisikletle on beş dakikada ulaşılabilir olmasını önerir. Herkesin evine yakın çalışmasını 'requires' (zorunlu kılmak) ettiği söylenmez; Barselona'nın süper blokları ('superblocks') kavramın ilk uygulaması değil, yalnızca 'related experiment' (benzer bir deneme) olarak anılır; emlak fiyatlarını ('property prices') düşürmek bir amaç değil, aksine fiyat artışı bir eleştiridir; yoğun Avrupa kentlerine daha uygun olduğu söylendiği için 'rejected' seçeneği yanlıştır.

questions.passage: The idea that daily life should be organised around short trips rather than long ones is hardly new, but it has gained remarkable momentum in recent years under the label of the '15-minute city'. Popularised by the urbanist Carlos Moreno, the concept proposes that residents should be able to reach most of what they need, from schools and shops to clinics, parks and workplaces, within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. Its appeal is easy to understand. Shorter journeys mean less traffic, cleaner air and more time for family and leisure, while busier local streets may support small businesses and strengthen a sense of community. Paris made the idea a central part of its planning agenda, converting parking spaces into cycle lanes and opening some school playgrounds to the public outside school hours. Barcelona's 'superblocks', in which groups of city blocks are closed to through traffic and their inner streets given over to pedestrians, are often cited as a related experiment. Yet the concept has also attracted criticism from several directions. Some planners note that it suits dense European cities far better than sprawling ones, where the population within a fifteen-minute radius may be too small to sustain a hospital or a secondary school. Others warn that improving a neighbourhood's amenities can push up property prices and gradually displace the very residents it was meant to serve. A third objection concerns employment: few people are free to choose a job simply because it is close to home. Supporters reply that the 15-minute city was never intended as a rigid rule but as a direction of travel, a way of asking which services could reasonably be brought closer to the people who use them.

Kavramın 'failed' (başarısız) olduğunu kabul etmezler; yasa ile 'enforced' edilmesini istemezler; hizmetlerin kent merkezine taşınması fikrin tersidir; eleştirileri 'justified' bulmak yerine onlara yanıt verirler.

questions.passage: On coral reefs across the Indian and Pacific oceans, small blue-and-black fish known as cleaner wrasse run what amount to roadside service stations. Larger fish, including species that would ordinarily eat a fish of this size, visit these cleaning stations, adopt special motionless postures and allow the wrasse to pick parasites and dead tissue from their skin, their gills and even the inside of their mouths. The arrangement is usually described as mutualism, a relationship in which both partners benefit: the client is relieved of parasites, while the cleaner obtains a reliable meal. Closer observation, however, has revealed that the relationship is far from simple. Cleaner wrasse actually prefer to eat the protective mucus that coats their clients' skin, and taking a bite of it, which makes the client jolt, amounts to cheating. Clients respond in various ways. Some chase a dishonest cleaner; others simply swim off and visit a different station next time. Remarkably, cleaners seem to adjust their behaviour accordingly. They tend to cheat less when they are being watched by other potential clients, and they treat visitors that could easily switch to another station more gently than resident fish that have no such choice. Such findings have led some researchers to argue that these small fish possess social skills once thought to be limited to primates and other large-brained animals. The ecological importance of the service is also considerable. In experiments in which cleaners were removed from patches of reef, the number and variety of fish visiting those patches tended to decline over time, suggesting that the activity of a single small species may help to sustain the diversity of an entire reef community.

questions.passage: For most of the past two thousand years, Hebrew was nobody's mother tongue. It survived as a language of prayer, law and scholarship, read and written by educated Jews across the world, but in everyday life they spoke Yiddish, Arabic, Ladino or the language of the country around them. Its return as a spoken language from the late nineteenth century onwards is often described as the only fully successful revival of a language that had lost its native speakers. The lexicographer Eliezer Ben-Yehuda is frequently credited with this achievement, and he did insist on speaking only Hebrew at home and devoted decades to coining words for modern objects and ideas. Many historians, however, argue that his personal role has been exaggerated. What proved decisive, they suggest, were the schools established in the agricultural settlements of Palestine, where teachers taught every subject through Hebrew, and the children who then made it the language of the playground and, eventually, of their own families. Once a generation had grown up using it for everything from games to quarrels, the language no longer depended on the enthusiasm of a few idealists. The result was not simply ancient Hebrew brought back to life. Modern Israeli Hebrew borrowed heavily from the languages its first speakers already knew, in pronunciation, idiom and even sentence structure, so that some linguists regard it as a partly new language rather than a restored old one. The Hebrew case is often cited by communities trying to strengthen endangered languages, from Welsh to Hawaiian. Yet its circumstances were unusual: settlers from many different backgrounds needed a common language, and Hebrew carried enormous symbolic weight for all of them. Revivalists elsewhere rarely enjoy both advantages, which helps to explain why their progress is usually slower.

questions.passage: When planners in Curitiba, in southern Brazil, set out to improve public transport in the 1970s, they lacked the money to build an underground railway. Their solution was to make buses behave as much like trains as possible. Dedicated lanes separated buses from other traffic, so that they were no longer held up in congestion. Later, passengers came to pay before boarding, inside distinctive tube-shaped stations raised to the level of the bus floor, which meant that dozens of people could step on at once instead of queuing past a driver. Long articulated vehicles carried large numbers of passengers, and the routes were combined with zoning rules that encouraged dense development along the main corridors. The result, which came to be known as bus rapid transit, offered much of the speed and capacity of a metro at a fraction of the cost. Over the following decades the model spread widely, with notable systems in Bogotá, Istanbul, Guangzhou and dozens of other cities. Its success, however, has not been uniform. Where the defining features are watered down, for instance when lanes are merely painted rather than physically separated, or when cars are allowed to use them at certain hours, buses tend to slow down and lose passengers. Popular systems face the opposite problem: they may become so crowded that passengers complain of conditions little better than those they had hoped to escape. Moreover, because a bus lane can be removed far more easily than a railway track, some critics argue that bus rapid transit sends a weaker signal to property developers, who may be reluctant to invest along a route that a future government could abandon. Even so, for fast-growing cities with limited budgets, it remains one of the most practical options available.

questions.explanation: Parçada bazı eleştirmenlerin, otobüs şeridinin raydan çok daha kolay kaldırılabildiği için geliştiricilerin bu güzergâhlara yatırım yapmakta isteksiz olabileceğini savunduğu belirtilir. Körüklü otobüslerin ('articulated buses') şeritlere sığmadığı söylenmez; sistemin metroya göre maliyetin 'fraction' (küçük bir kısmı) olduğu belirtildiği için daha pahalı olduğu iddiası yanlıştır; imar kuralları ('zoning rules') yoğun yapılaşmayı engellemek ('prevent') bir yana 'encouraged' (teşvik etmek) etmiştir; model Bogota, İstanbul ve Guangzhou gibi birçok kente 'adopted' edilmiştir.

questions.passage: When planners in Curitiba, in southern Brazil, set out to improve public transport in the 1970s, they lacked the money to build an underground railway. Their solution was to make buses behave as much like trains as possible. Dedicated lanes separated buses from other traffic, so that they were no longer held up in congestion. Later, passengers came to pay before boarding, inside distinctive tube-shaped stations raised to the level of the bus floor, which meant that dozens of people could step on at once instead of queuing past a driver. Long articulated vehicles carried large numbers of passengers, and the routes were combined with zoning rules that encouraged dense development along the main corridors. The result, which came to be known as bus rapid transit, offered much of the speed and capacity of a metro at a fraction of the cost. Over the following decades the model spread widely, with notable systems in Bogotá, Istanbul, Guangzhou and dozens of other cities. Its success, however, has not been uniform. Where the defining features are watered down, for instance when lanes are merely painted rather than physically separated, or when cars are allowed to use them at certain hours, buses tend to slow down and lose passengers. Popular systems face the opposite problem: they may become so crowded that passengers complain of conditions little better than those they had hoped to escape. Moreover, because a bus lane can be removed far more easily than a railway track, some critics argue that bus rapid transit sends a weaker signal to property developers, who may be reluctant to invest along a route that a future government could abandon. Even so, for fast-growing cities with limited budgets, it remains one of the most practical options available.
questions.text: The author's overall view of bus rapid transit is that it ----.
options: has failed in almost every city that has tried to adopt it
should eventually replace all underground railways
is too expensive for cities in developing countries
has become popular only in the country where it began
is a practical solution for many cities, although it works well only when its key features are kept intact
questions.explanation: Yazar sistemin başarısının her yerde aynı olmadığını, temel özellikleri zayıflatıldığında otobüslerin yavaşladığını belirtir ama son cümlede hızla büyüyen ve bütçesi sınırlı kentler için en pratik seçeneklerden biri olduğunu söyler. Hemen her kentte 'failed' (başarısız) olduğu söylenmez; tüm metroların yerini 'replace' etmesi önerilmez; düşük maliyeti vurgulandığı için 'expensive' seçeneği yanlıştır; model birçok ülkeye yayıldığından yalnızca Brezilya'da 'popular' olduğu iddiası da yanlıştır.

questions.passage: In the late nineteenth century, beriberi, a disease that causes weakness, nerve damage and, in severe cases, heart failure, was widespread in parts of Asia where polished white rice formed the bulk of the diet. Decades later, the anthropologist Victor Turner (3) ---- particular attention to the middle stage, which he described as 'liminal', from the Latin word for threshold. During this period, initiates are often stripped of their usual clothing, names or possessions and treated (4) ---- equals, a condition that Turner believed could generate intense bonds of solidarity. (5) ---- the ceremonies themselves may have declined in many modern societies, scholars have identified traces of the same pattern in events such as university graduations and military training.

questions.text: Just as some cultures regard insects as a delicacy, ----.

others consider eating them to be unthinkable
which explains why insect farms are spreading quickly
although they contain more protein than beef
if farmers raise them in large numbers
questions.explanation: ‘Just as …’ (nasıl ki …) iki kültürel tutumu yan yana koyan bir ana cümle ister: bazı kültürler böcekleri lezzet sayar, diğerleri yemeyi ‘unthinkable’ bulur. ‘Because … rich in protein’, ‘although … beef’ ve ‘insect farms are spreading’ diye biten ilgi cümlesi ana cümle kurmaz; ‘if farmers raise them’ ise karşılaştırmayı tamamlamaz.

questions.text: The new battery can be recharged thousands of times without losing capacity, ----.
options: making it suitable for storing energy from solar panels over many years
although it can only be used once
unless the battery was invented
so that it had been tested
whose capacity is lost quickly
questions.explanation: Binlerce kez şarj edilebilmesi pili güneş enerjisini yıllarca depolamaya uygun kılar; ‘making it suitable’ bu sonucu bildirir. ‘Only be used once’ ve ‘capacity is lost quickly’ cümleyle çelişir; ‘unless … invented’ ve ‘had been tested’ ise anlamsızdır ve zaman bakımından uyuşmaz.

questions.text: Unless people who follow a strictly plant-based diet take supplements or eat fortified foods, ----.
options: they had eaten plenty of fresh vegetables
because plants contain all the nutrients that humans need
the vitamin was first isolated in the 1940s
although fortified cereals are widely available
they may develop a deficiency of vitamin B12, which is found almost exclusively in animal products
questions.explanation: ‘Unless’ ile kurulan gerçek koşul olası bir sonuç ister: takviye almayan bitkisel beslenenlerde B12 eksikliği gelişebilir. ‘Had eaten … vegetables’ zaman bakımından uyuşmaz; ‘because plants contain all the nutrients’ ve ‘although fortified cereals’ ana cümle değildir; vitaminin ilk kez ‘isolated’ edildiği tarih ise koşulla ilgisizdir.

questions.text: So rapidly did the new alloy corrode in seawater ----.

which surprised the engineers who had designed it
as if it were made of ordinary iron
even though it had been coated with paint
that the company had to withdraw it from the market within a year

questions.text: The tribe's oral traditions, ----, describe a great flood that forced their ancestors to move inland.

although they were written down
whose members moved inland
because the river flooded frequently
which have been passed down from one generation to the next for centuries

so that their metabolism will slow down

as long as they had skipped breakfast
whereas the human stomach was empty in the morning

questions.text:
Aşağıdaki İngilizce cümlenin anlamca en yakın Türkçe karşılığı hangisidir?

Yerkabuğunda bol bulunmasına rağmen alüminyumun çıkarılması bugün altınınkinden daha zordur.

questions.text:
Aşağıdaki İngilizce cümlenin anlamca en yakın Türkçe karşılığı hangisidir?

It was not until the invention of refrigeration that fresh meat could be transported over long distances without spoiling.
options: Soğutmanın icadı, taze etin uzun mesafelere taşınmasını zorlaştırdı.
Taze et, soğutma icat edilmeden önce de bozulmadan uzun mesafelere taşınabiliyordu.

Taze et, ancak soğutmanın icadından sonra bozulmadan uzun mesafelere taşınabildi.

Taşımayı ‘zorlaştırdı’ diyen çeviri anlamı tersine çevirir; icattan ‘önce de’ taşınabildiğini söyleyen ve icattan sonra ‘bile’ bozulduğunu söyleyen çeviriler özgün cümleyle çelişir; taşımanın icada ‘yol açmıştır’ demek ise neden-sonuç ilişkisini tersine çevirir.

Aşağıdaki İngilizce cümlenin anlamca en yakın Türkçe karşılığı hangisidir?

The more closely anthropologists study so-called simple societies, the more complex their systems of kinship and exchange turn out to be.

Antropologlar, basit toplumların değiş tokuş sistemlerini, akrabalık sistemlerinden daha yakından incelemektedir.
Sözde basit toplumlar ne kadar karmaşıklaşırsa, antropologlar onları o kadar yakından incelemektedir.

Doğru çeviri ‘ne kadar yakından incelerse … o kadar karmaşık çıkmaktadır’ diye kurulan cümledir. Akrabalığı değiş tokuştan daha karmaşık ‘görürler’ diyen çeviri karşılaştırmayı değiştirir; incelemeyi ‘zorlaştıracak’ kadar karmaşık diyen çeviri sonuç ilişkisi ekler; ‘daha yakından incelemektedir’ diyen çeviri iki sistemi karşılaştırır; toplumlar ‘karmaşıklaşırsa’ diyen çeviri ise ilişkiyi tersine çevirir.

Aşağıdaki Türkçe cümlenin anlamca en yakın İngilizce karşılığı hangisidir?

Mayalanma sırasında bakteriler sütteki şekeri asite dönüştürür ve bu da ürünün daha uzun süre bozulmadan kalmasını sağlar.
options: Bacteria convert milk into sugar during fermentation, so the product spoils more quickly.

Because the product remains unspoiled for longer, bacteria can convert the acid in milk into sugar.
During fermentation, the acid in milk prevents bacteria from converting sugar, which is why the product spoils.

Şebekelerin zaten modernize edildiğini söyleyen ‘thanks to’ çevirisi anlamı değiştirir; ‘will fail even if’ koşulu tersine çevirir; ‘more important than switching’ bir karşılaştırma ekler; ‘abandoned’ içeren çeviri ise yenilenebilir kaynakların terk edilmesinden söz eder.

Aşağıdaki Türkçe cümlenin anlamca en yakın İngilizce karşılığı hangisidir?

Göçebe topluluklar, yanlarında taşıyabilecekleri eşya sayısı sınırlı olduğundan, genellikle mülkiyete yerleşik toplumlardan farklı bir anlam yükler.
options: Nomadic communities generally own more property than settled societies, even though they cannot carry many belongings.
Because settled societies have limited belongings, they attach less meaning to property than nomadic communities do.

questions.passage:
On a clear night, any surface exposed to the sky loses heat by emitting infrared radiation, which is why frost can form on a car roof even when the surrounding air remains slightly above freezing. Much of this radiation escapes through the atmosphere into the cold of outer space, mainly at wavelengths between about eight and thirteen micrometres, a range in which the air is largely transparent. For centuries, people in hot, dry regions exploited this effect, leaving shallow pools of water outdoors overnight so that thin layers of ice could be collected before sunrise.
Achieving the same cooling during the day had long been considered impractical, because sunlight delivers far more energy to a surface than it can radiate away. Over the past decade, however, materials scientists have developed coatings that overcome this obstacle. These materials combine two properties: they reflect almost all incoming sunlight, and they emit strongly within the atmospheric window. Some consist of carefully layered films, whereas others are paints filled with particles that scatter visible light. Under direct sunshine, the best of them have been reported to remain several degrees cooler than the surrounding air without consuming any electricity.
The potential benefits are considerable, since air conditioning already accounts for a significant share of electricity demand in many hot countries and is expected to grow. Applied to roofs, such coatings could reduce the need for mechanical cooling, particularly in low-rise buildings. Nevertheless, researchers caution against excessive optimism. Performance declines sharply in humid or cloudy conditions, when water vapour blocks part of the window, and dust or dirt can quickly diminish reflectivity. Moreover, in cold climates, a surface that cools itself all year round might actually raise heating costs in winter, so some teams are now designing materials whose properties change with temperature.
questions.text: The passage mainly discusses ----.
options: materials that allow surfaces to stay cooler than the air in daylight, together with their promise and limitations
the history of ice production in hot and dry regions
why air conditioning consumes more electricity in humid climates
the effect of clouds and water vapour on global temperatures
a new method of heating buildings in cold climates
questions.explanation: Metin gece ışınımla soğumayı açıklar, ardından gün ışığında havadan serin kalabilen kaplamaları, yararlarını ve sınırlılıklarını anlatır; ana konu ‘promise and limitations’ ile biten seçenektir. Buz üretiminin ‘history’si yalnızca bir örnektir; klimanın nemli iklimde daha çok elektrik tüketmesi (‘humid climates’) ve bulutların küresel sıcaklığa etkisi (‘global temperatures’) metnin konusu değildir; binaları ‘heating’ yöntemi ise anlatılmaz.

questions.text: The author's attitude towards radiative cooling coatings can best be described as ----.

entirely dismissive
openly hostile
deeply indifferent

questions.passage:
Hempcrete is a building material made by mixing the woody inner core of the hemp plant, known as shiv or hurd, with a lime-based binder and water. Once the mixture has been packed into a timber frame, the lime gradually hardens by absorbing carbon dioxide from the air, a process that continues for months and, according to some estimates, even years. The result is a lightweight wall that weighs roughly one-eighth as much as conventional concrete. Unlike concrete, however, hempcrete cannot bear heavy loads, so it is used to fill and insulate walls rather than to hold a building up.
Supporters emphasise the material's environmental credentials. Hemp grows quickly, often needs little or no pesticide and absorbs carbon dioxide while it grows, and part of this carbon remains locked inside the finished wall. When the carbon absorbed by the lime is also taken into account, several life-cycle analyses have concluded that a hempcrete wall may store more carbon than was released in manufacturing and transporting it, although the figures depend heavily on assumptions about farming methods and the production of the lime, which itself requires heating limestone to high temperatures.
Hempcrete also regulates indoor conditions in ways that builders value. Because it is porous, it absorbs moisture when the air is humid and releases it when the air is dry, which helps keep humidity stable and reduces the risk of mould. Its thermal mass slows the movement of heat through walls, smoothing out temperature changes between day and night.
The obstacles to its wider use are largely practical rather than technical. Walls cast on site can take weeks to dry, building regulations in many countries do not yet cover the material, and in places where cultivating hemp has long been restricted because of its association with the drug-producing varieties of cannabis, supply chains remain underdeveloped.
questions.text: According to the passage, hempcrete is used to fill walls rather than to support buildings because ----.
options: it absorbs too much moisture from the air
it takes several years to harden completely
building regulations forbid its use in load-bearing walls
it is much heavier than conventional concrete
it is not strong enough to carry heavy loads
questions.explanation: Birinci paragrafta kenevir betonunun ağır yük taşıyamadığı (‘cannot bear heavy loads’) için duvarları doldurmakta kullanıldığı söylenir; doğru seçenek ‘not strong enough’ diye başlar. Nem emmesi (‘moisture’) üçüncü paragrafta bir avantajdır; sertleşmenin yıllar sürebilmesi (‘harden completely’) gerekçe olarak verilmez; yönetmeliklerin malzemeyi kapsamadığı söylenir ama bir yasaktan (‘forbid’) söz edilmez; malzeme betondan ‘heavier’ değil çok daha hafiftir.

questions.passage:
Hempcrete is a building material made by mixing the woody inner core of the hemp plant, known as shiv or hurd, with a lime-based binder and water. Once the mixture has been packed into a timber frame, the lime gradually hardens by absorbing carbon dioxide from the air, a process that continues for months and, according to some estimates, even years. The result is a lightweight wall that weighs roughly one-eighth as much as conventional concrete. Unlike concrete, however, hempcrete cannot bear heavy loads, so it is used to fill and insulate walls rather than to hold a building up.
Supporters emphasise the material's environmental credentials. Hemp grows quickly, often needs little or no pesticide and absorbs carbon dioxide while it grows, and part of this carbon remains locked inside the finished wall. When the carbon absorbed by the lime is also taken into account, several life-cycle analyses have concluded that a hempcrete wall may store more carbon than was released in manufacturing and transporting it, although the figures depend heavily on assumptions about farming methods and the production of the lime, which itself requires heating limestone to high temperatures.
Hempcrete also regulates indoor conditions in ways that builders value. Because it is porous, it absorbs moisture when the air is humid and releases it when the air is dry, which helps keep humidity stable and reduces the risk of mould. Its thermal mass slows the movement of heat through walls, smoothing out temperature changes between day and night.
The obstacles to its wider use are largely practical rather than technical. Walls cast on site can take weeks to dry, building regulations in many countries do not yet cover the material, and in places where cultivating hemp has long been restricted because of its association with the drug-producing varieties of cannabis, supply chains remain underdeveloped.

questions.passage:
It seems intuitive that people who are physically active burn far more energy each day than those who spend most of their time sitting, and that exercise should therefore be a powerful tool for losing weight. Measurements of total daily energy expenditure, however, have produced a more puzzling picture. Using a technique based on water labelled with rare isotopes, which allows the energy a person uses over one or two weeks to be estimated from urine samples, researchers have compared groups with strikingly different lifestyles. Among the most widely discussed findings are those from the Hadza, a community of hunter-gatherers in northern Tanzania who walk long distances every day in search of food. Despite this high level of activity, the average Hadza adult appears to burn roughly the same number of calories per day as an adult in an industrialised country, once differences in body size are taken into account.
To explain such results, some scientists have proposed that the body operates within a constrained energy budget. When physical activity increases, the body may compensate by reducing the energy it devotes to other processes, such as inflammation, the production of certain hormones or the repair of tissues. In the short term, a new exercise programme does raise expenditure, but over months the increase tends to be smaller than simple calculations would predict.
The hypothesis does not imply that exercise is pointless. On the contrary, its proponents suggest that by diverting energy away from chronic inflammation, regular activity may be one reason why active people suffer less from heart disease and other illnesses. What it does challenge is the assumption that people can reliably offset a high-calorie diet simply by being more active, which implies that weight management depends more on what and how much we eat. Critics note, however, that the degree of compensation varies widely between individuals and that the evidence is still being debated.

questions.passage:
Compared with many other mammals, humans are poor sprinters: a horse, a dog or even a goat can easily outpace the fastest athlete over a short distance. Over long distances in hot weather, however, people can match or even outlast most animals, and some researchers believe that this ability played a central role in human evolution. According to the endurance running hypothesis, early members of the genus Homo may have obtained meat partly through persistence hunting, chasing an animal during the hottest part of the day until it collapsed from exhaustion and overheating.
Proponents point to a cluster of anatomical features that seem well suited to this activity. Long tendons in the legs, including the Achilles tendon, store and release elastic energy with each stride, and the large gluteal muscles stabilise the trunk when running rather than walking. Above all, humans are exceptionally efficient at shedding heat. With little body hair and millions of sweat glands, a runner can cool down while still moving, whereas most four-legged animals must stop and pant to lower their body temperature.
The hypothesis has nonetheless attracted considerable criticism. Sceptics argue that tracking an animal for hours would have required sophisticated knowledge of its behaviour and footprints, skills that might have developed only much later. Others note that persistence hunting has been documented among only a handful of recent groups, such as some San hunters of the Kalahari, and that even they appear to use it rarely. It is also possible that several of the features in question evolved for walking efficiently over long distances and only later proved useful for running.
Whatever its ultimate fate, the debate has encouraged researchers to consider how physical endurance, and not merely intelligence or tool use, may have shaped the human body.

questions.passage:
Cassava, a starchy root native to South America, is today a staple food for hundreds of millions of people in the tropics, valued because it tolerates poor soils and drought and can be left in the ground for many months until it is needed. Yet many varieties, particularly the so-called bitter ones, contain compounds that release hydrogen cyanide when the plant's tissues are damaged. Eaten raw or poorly prepared, these varieties can cause acute poisoning and, if consumed regularly over long periods, chronic conditions affecting the nerves.
Indigenous peoples in the Amazon basin developed elaborate methods of removing the toxins long before their chemistry was understood. In one widespread technique, the roots are peeled and grated, the pulp is squeezed in long woven tubes to remove the liquid, and the remaining mash is left to stand for some time before being dried and cooked. Several of these steps appear unnecessary at first sight, since the bitter taste largely disappears early in the process. Chemical analyses, however, suggest that each stage removes or breaks down a further portion of the toxic compounds, and that skipping any of them can leave dangerous amounts behind.
Some anthropologists regard such practices as a striking example of cultural knowledge that works even though those who follow it cannot explain why. Because the effects of chronic cyanide exposure may appear only after years, it would be very difficult for any single individual to discover the correct procedure through trial and error. When cassava was introduced to Africa from the sixteenth century onwards, by contrast, it seems that the full processing traditions did not always travel with it, and in some regions where diets depend heavily on insufficiently processed roots, outbreaks of cyanide-related disease still occur, particularly during droughts and food shortages.

Eaten raw or poorly prepared, these varieties can cause acute poisoning and, if consumed regularly over long periods, chronic conditions affecting the nerves.
Indigenous peoples in the Amazon basin developed elaborate methods of removing the toxins long before their chemistry was understood. In one widespread technique, the roots are peeled and grated, the pulp is squeezed in long woven tubes to remove the liquid, and the remaining mash is left to stand for some time before being dried and cooked. Several of these steps appear unnecessary at first sight, since the bitter taste largely disappears early in the process. Chemical analyses, however, suggest that each stage removes or breaks down a further portion of the toxic compounds, and that skipping any of them can leave dangerous amounts behind.
Some anthropologists regard such practices as a striking example of cultural knowledge that works even though those who follow it cannot explain why. Because the effects of chronic cyanide exposure may appear only after years, it would be very difficult for any single individual to discover the correct procedure through trial and error. When cassava was introduced to Africa from the sixteenth century onwards, by contrast, it seems that the full processing traditions did not always travel with it, and in some regions where diets depend heavily on insufficiently processed roots, outbreaks of cyanide-related disease still occur, particularly during droughts and food shortages.

options: warn readers against eating cassava in any form
show that acute poisoning is more dangerous than chronic illness
prove that Amazonian peoples understood the chemistry of cyanide
argue that cassava should not have been introduced to Africa
explain why the processing methods are unlikely to have been discovered by individuals experimenting alone

questions.explanation: Paragraf And dağlarında patatesin dondurulup kurutularak saklandığı chuño yöntemini, ürünün özelliklerini ve kıtlığa karşı sağladığı korumayı anlatır. V numaralı cümle patatesin Avrupa’ya gelişine geçerek bu saklama yönteminden sapar. I yöntemi tanıtır, II işlemi açıklar, III ‘The resulting product’ ile ortaya çıkan ürünü, IV ise ‘such stores’ ile bu stokların yüksek rakımlı topluluklar için önemini anlatır.

questions.text: Over the past two decades, the sheer volume of data produced by modern telescopes has ---- the capacity of astronomers to analyse it by hand, prompting a turn towards automated methods.
options: deprived
consoled
retrieved
outstripped
endorsed
questions.explanation: ‘Outstripped’ (aşmak, geride bırakmak) verinin, gökbilimcilerin elle çözümleme kapasitesini aştığını anlatır; ‘prompting a turn towards automated methods’ bu yüzden otomatik yöntemlere geçildiğini gösterir. ‘Deprived’ (yoksun bırakmak), ‘consoled’ (teselli etmek), ‘retrieved’ (geri almak) ve ‘endorsed’ (onaylamak) veri ile kapasite arasındaki bu ilişkiyi kurmaz.

questions.text: Public-health officials argue that high taxes on tobacco are ---- because they discourage smoking among young people, who are particularly sensitive to changes in price.
options: negligible
justified
redundant
hostile
obsolete
questions.explanation: Yetkililer vergilerin gençleri sigaradan caydırdığını gerekçe olarak gösterir; bu gerekçe vergilerin ‘justified’ (haklı, yerinde) olduğu savunusuna uyar. ‘Negligible’ (önemsiz), ‘redundant’ (gereksiz), ‘hostile’ (düşmanca) ve ‘obsolete’ (modası geçmiş) ‘because they discourage smoking’ gerekçesiyle çelişir ya da anlamsız kalır.

questions.text: The collapse of several large banks in the early 1930s ---- a wave of panic in which ordinary depositors rushed to withdraw their savings.
options: alleviated
concealed
inhibited
triggered
overlooked
questions.explanation: Bankaların çökmesi, mevduat sahiplerinin paralarını çekmeye koştuğu bir panik dalgasını ‘triggered’ (tetiklemek) etmiştir. ‘Alleviated’ (hafifletmek) ve ‘inhibited’ (engellemek) paniğin ortaya çıkmasıyla çelişir; ‘concealed’ (gizlemek) ve ‘overlooked’ (gözden kaçırmak) çöküş ile panik arasındaki neden-sonuç ilişkisini anlatmaz.

questions.text: The effects of the new vaccination policy were ---- apparent within a year: hospital admissions for measles fell by more than half in the regions where it was applied.
options: barely
reluctantly
vaguely
readily
seldom
questions.explanation: İki noktadan sonra gelen güçlü kanıt (hastaneye yatışların yarıdan fazla düşmesi) etkilerin bir yıl içinde ‘readily’ (kolayca, açıkça) görülebildiğini gösterir. ‘Barely’ (güçlükle) ve ‘vaguely’ (belli belirsiz) bu güçlü düşüşle çelişir; ‘reluctantly’ (isteksizce) bir etki için kullanılmaz; ‘seldom’ (nadiren) ise tek bir yıl içindeki sonuca uymaz.

questions.text: When the price of grain rose sharply after a series of poor harvests, many families were forced to ---- spending on everything except food.
options: look up
give off
cut back
bring about
take after
questions.explanation: Tahıl fiyatı yükselince aileler yiyecek dışındaki harcamaları kısmak zorunda kalır; bu anlam ‘cut back’ (kısmak, azaltmak) ile verilir. ‘Look up’ (sözlükte aramak), ‘give off’ (yaymak), ‘bring about’ (neden olmak) ve ‘take after’ (birine benzemek) harcamalarla birlikte bu bağlamda anlam taşımaz.

questions.text: ---- the dangers of travelling through lawless territory, medieval merchants continued to carry goods across Europe, since the profits could be enormous.
options: Owing to
In addition to
Notwithstanding
Instead of
By means of
questions.explanation: Tehlikelere karşın tüccarların ticarete devam etmesi bir karşıtlık bildirir; bu karşıtlığı ‘Notwithstanding’ (-e rağmen) kurar. ‘Owing to’ (yüzünden) tehlikeyi devam etmenin nedeni yapar; ‘In addition to’ (-e ek olarak), ‘Instead of’ (yerine) ve ‘By means of’ (aracılığıyla) cümlenin mantığına uymaz.

questions.text: By the time the probe reaches the outer edge of the solar system, it ---- through space for more than twenty years.
options: will have been travelling
has travelled
would travel
had been travelling
travels
questions.explanation: ‘By the time … reaches’ gelecekteki bir noktayı gösterir; o ana kadar sürmüş olacak eylem için ‘will have been travelling’ gerekir. ‘Has travelled’ şimdiye, ‘had been travelling’ geçmişe bağlanır; ‘would travel’ ve ‘travels’ ise süreklilik ve tamamlanmışlık anlamını vermez.

questions.text: The comet, ---- was first recorded by Chinese astronomers more than two thousand years ago, returns to the inner solar system roughly every 76 years.
options: which
whose
where
what
that
questions.explanation: Virgülle ayrılan, ‘The comet’ adını niteleyen ve öznesi olmayan bir ilgi cümlesi gerekir; ‘which’ doğrudur. ‘That’ virgüllü (non-defining) ilgi cümlelerinde kullanılmaz; ‘whose’ arkasından bir isim ister; ‘where’ yer bildirir; ‘what’ ise bir ismi niteleyemez.

questions.text: Many economic historians believe that if the authorities ---- more money into the banking system in the early 1930s, the depression would have been far less severe.
options: injected
had injected
have injected
would inject
were injecting
questions.explanation: Ana cümledeki ‘would have been’ geçmişe ait gerçekleşmemiş bir koşulu (third conditional) gösterir; ‘if’ cümlesinde ‘had injected’ gerekir. ‘Injected’ ve ‘were injecting’ ikinci tip koşula aittir; ‘have injected’ şimdiki zamana bağlanır; ‘would inject’ ise ‘if’ cümlesinde kullanılmaz.

questions.text: Before a new vaccine is approved for general use, it ---- in large clinical trials involving thousands of volunteers.
options: must test
has tested
must be tested
should have tested
is testing
questions.explanation: Aşı test eden değil test edilen nesnedir; bu yüzden edilgen ve zorunluluk bildiren ‘must be tested’ gerekir. ‘Must test’, ‘has tested’, ‘should have tested’ ve ‘is testing’ etken yapılardır ve aşıyı testi yapan özne konumuna sokar.

questions.text: It was only after the bank had collapsed ---- investors realised how much of its money had been lent to its own directors.
options: that
which
since
what
whereby
questions.explanation: ‘It was only after … that …’ vurgu (cleft) yapısıdır; boşluğa ‘that’ gelir. ‘Which’ ve ‘what’ bu yapıda kullanılmaz; ‘since’ ve ‘whereby’ ise ‘It was only after’ ile başlayan kalıbı tamamlamaz.

questions.text: ---- the high cost of the programme, the government decided to extend free cancer screening to all adults over fifty.
options: Despite
Although
Because of
Unless
Even though
questions.explanation: Boşluktan sonra yalnızca bir isim öbeği (‘the high cost of the programme’) gelir ve maliyete karşın genişletme kararı bir karşıtlıktır; ‘Despite’ doğrudur. ‘Although’, ‘Even though’ ve ‘Unless’ arkalarından bir yan cümle ister; ‘Because of’ ise yüksek maliyeti genişletme kararının nedeni yapar.

questions.text: The authorities had promised a stronger currency, but hardly ---- the new coins when merchants began to complain that they contained less silver than expected.
options: they had issued
would they issue
have they issued
they issued
had they issued
questions.explanation: ‘Hardly’ devrik yapı ister ve ‘when’ ile birlikte geçmişte bir olayın hemen ardından ötekinin geldiğini anlatır; ‘had they issued’ gerekir. ‘They had issued’ ve ‘they issued’ devrik değildir; ‘have they issued’ şimdiki zamana bağlanır; ‘would they issue’ ise geçmişteki bu ardışıklığı anlatmaz.

questions.text: Not only ---- the number of people seeking treatment, but it also reduced the stigma attached to the illness.
options: the campaign increased
did the campaign increase
the campaign has increased
would the campaign have increased
increased the campaign
questions.explanation: Cümle başındaki ‘Not only’ devrik yapı ister ve ikinci kısım ‘reduced’ ile geçmiş zamandadır; ‘did the campaign increase’ doğrudur. ‘The campaign increased’ ve ‘the campaign has increased’ devrik değildir; ‘would the campaign have increased’ gerçekleşmemiş bir durum anlatır; ‘increased the campaign’ ise özne ile nesneyi karıştırır.

questions.text: The success of the policy depends largely ---- whether local health workers are trusted by the communities they serve.
options: on
with
for
at
from
questions.explanation: ‘Depend’ fiili ‘on’ edatıyla kullanılır (depend on: -e bağlı olmak). ‘With’, ‘for’, ‘at’ ve ‘from’ bu fiille kalıp oluşturmaz.

questions.text: The more carefully the surviving records are examined, ---- it becomes that the famine was caused by policy rather than by drought.
options: clearer
the clearest
more clear
the clearer
the most clearly
questions.explanation: ‘The more …, the …’ karşılaştırma yapısında ikinci kısım da ‘the’ ile başlayan bir karşılaştırma sıfatı ister; ‘the clearer’ doğrudur. ‘Clearer’ ve ‘more clear’ ‘the’ almaz; ‘the clearest’ en üstünlük derecesidir; ‘the most clearly’ ise ‘becomes’ fiilinden sonra sıfat yerine zarf kullanır.

questions.passage: For most of history, astronomers had no reliable way of knowing how far away the stars were. The principle that eventually (1) ---- the problem is surprisingly simple: as the Earth moves around the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against the background of much more distant ones, and the size of this shift reveals its distance. In practice, however, the effect is so tiny that it eluded observers for centuries; even the closest stars shift by less than one second of arc, (2) ---- is roughly the width of a coin seen from several kilometres away. It was only in 1838 that the German astronomer Friedrich Bessel finally (3) ---- in measuring such a shift, for a faint star in the constellation Cygnus. Progress afterwards remained slow, (4) ---- the Earth's atmosphere blurs starlight and limits the precision of ground-based instruments. Space telescopes have removed this obstacle, and a recent mission has measured the positions of more than a billion stars, (5) ---- astronomers to build the most detailed three-dimensional map of our galaxy ever produced.
questions.text: (1) numaralı boşluğa hangisi gelmelidir?
options: postponed
concealed
exaggerated
solved
abandoned
questions.explanation: Paragraf yıldız uzaklığı sorununun sonunda nasıl çözüldüğünü anlatır; ‘eventually solved the problem’ (sonunda sorunu çözen ilke) doğrudur. ‘Postponed’ (ertelemek), ‘concealed’ (gizlemek), ‘exaggerated’ (abartmak) ve ‘abandoned’ (bırakmak) bir ilkenin sorunla ilişkisini anlatmaz ve paragrafın akışıyla çelişir.

questions.passage: Alcohol impairs the skills required for safe driving long before a person feels drunk, slowing reaction times and (1) ---- the ability to judge speed and distance. For this reason, most countries set a legal limit on the concentration of alcohol in a driver's blood, although the level chosen varies considerably from one country to another. Several European countries have lowered their limit in recent decades, and evaluations of these changes generally suggest that road deaths fell (2) ----, particularly among young and inexperienced drivers. Critics, however, argue that stricter limits mainly punish moderate drinkers, (3) ---- the most dangerous drivers are those far above any limit. Research indicates that a lower limit works best when it (4) ---- by frequent random testing, since drivers who believe they are unlikely to be stopped tend to ignore the law. Public-health experts therefore regard legal limits not as a solution in themselves (5) ---- as one part of a broader strategy that includes enforcement and public education.

questions.text: Although the Moon appears to shine with a light of its own, ----.
options: because its surface is covered with a layer of fine dust
whose craters were formed by ancient impacts
it merely reflects light that reaches it from the Sun
the Earth's tides are largely caused by its gravity
so astronauts first walked on its surface in 1969
questions.explanation: ‘Although’ bir karşıtlık ister: Ay kendi ışığıyla parlıyor gibi görünse de yalnızca Güneş’ten gelen ışığı yansıtır. ‘Because’ ile başlayan cümle ve ‘whose craters’ ilgi cümlesi ana cümle kurmaz; gelgitlerin (‘tides’) Ay’ın kütleçekiminden kaynaklanması ve astronotların Ay’a inmesi (‘astronauts’) görünür ışıkla karşıtlık oluşturmaz.

questions.text: ----, the researchers concluded that the fall in road deaths could not be attributed to the new speed cameras alone.
options: Unless the cameras are moved to more dangerous roads
So that more drivers would respect the speed limits
Even if drivers had been warned about the cameras in advance
Whereas most drivers supported the use of cameras
Since road deaths had already been falling for several years before the cameras were installed
questions.explanation: Ölümler kameralar kurulmadan önce de düşüyorsa düşüş yalnızca kameralara bağlanamaz; neden bildiren ‘Since … had already been falling’ cümlesi doğrudur. ‘Unless … moved’ şimdi/gelecek koşuludur; ‘So that … respect’ amaç bildirir ve sonuca bağlanmaz; ‘Even if … warned’ ve sürücülerin desteğini anlatan ‘supported’ ise araştırmacıların vardığı sonucu açıklamaz.

questions.text: In the sixteenth century, large quantities of silver flowed into Europe from the Americas, ----.
options: although silver coins are rarely used today
if Spanish ships had not been attacked by pirates
so that gold became completely worthless
whereas the population of Europe has been declining since then
which contributed to a long period of rising prices
questions.explanation: Amerika’dan gelen büyük miktarda gümüş, uzun süreli bir fiyat artışına katkıda bulunmuştur; önceki cümlenin tamamını niteleyen ‘which contributed to … rising prices’ doğrudur. ‘Although … rarely used today’ ve ‘has been declining’ zaman ve anlam bakımından uymaz; ‘if … had not been attacked’ ana cümlesiz bir koşuldur; altının tümüyle değersiz (‘worthless’) olması ise yanlış ve abartılı bir sonuçtur.

questions.text: Scarcely had the bank opened its doors that morning ----.
options: when crowds of anxious depositors began demanding their money
than the government had guaranteed all deposits
so the manager decided to call the police
because rumours of its collapse were spreading
that it had lost most of its reserves
questions.explanation: ‘Scarcely had …’ yapısı ‘when’ ile tamamlanır ve bir olayın hemen ardından ötekinin geldiğini anlatır: Banka kapılarını açar açmaz endişeli mudiler paralarını istemeye başlamıştır. ‘Than’ bu yapıda kullanılmaz (‘no sooner … than’ ile karışır); ‘so the manager’, ‘because rumours’ ve ‘that it had lost’ ‘scarcely … when’ kalıbını tamamlamaz.

questions.text: Governments are often reluctant to raise taxes on alcohol ----.
options: until the first large breweries were built
since such measures tend to be unpopular with voters
as if the drinks were sold only in pharmacies

Sunspots are dark, relatively cool regions on the surface of the Sun, produced where intense magnetic fields inhibit the flow of heat from the interior. Their number rises and falls over a cycle of roughly eleven years, and because periods with many sunspots coincide with a slightly brighter Sun overall, they serve as a convenient index of solar activity. Telescopic records of sunspots extend back to the early seventeenth century, making them one of the longest continuous series of scientific observations in existence.
These records contain a striking anomaly. Between about 1645 and 1715, sunspots almost vanished; in some years observers reported none at all, although the instruments and techniques of the time were perfectly capable of detecting them. The episode is now known as the Maunder Minimum, after the astronomer who drew attention to it in the late nineteenth century. Independent evidence supports its reality: certain radioactive isotopes that form when cosmic rays strike the atmosphere, and which become more abundant when the Sun's magnetic shield weakens, increased markedly in tree rings and ice cores laid down during these decades.
The Maunder Minimum overlapped with one of the coldest phases of the so-called Little Ice Age, when harsh winters were recorded across much of Europe, and it has frequently been cited as evidence that the Sun drives the Earth's climate. Most climate scientists, however, treat this conclusion with caution. The cooling had begun before the sunspots disappeared, it was not uniform across the globe, and several large volcanic eruptions during the same period could account for much of it. Estimates of the reduction in solar output suggest a cooling of only a few tenths of a degree, which is noticeable but far smaller than the warming observed since the late twentieth century.

questions.passage:
In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, a cycle of six fairs held in the county of Champagne, in north-eastern France, became the principal meeting point of European commerce. Merchants from Italy brought spices, silk and dyes obtained in the eastern Mediterranean, while traders from Flanders arrived with the woollen cloth for which their towns were famous. The fairs owed their success less to geography than to policy. The counts of Champagne guaranteed safe conduct to travelling merchants, levied moderate tolls and appointed special officials, the 'guards of the fairs', who enforced contracts and could pursue defaulting debtors even beyond the county's borders.
Perhaps the most lasting legacy of the fairs, however, was financial. Because each fair ended with a period devoted exclusively to settling accounts, merchants increasingly found it unnecessary to carry large sums of coin, which were heavy and vulnerable to theft. Instead, debts were recorded and offset against one another, and only the remaining balances were paid. Out of this practice grew the bill of exchange, a written order instructing an agent in another city to pay a specified sum, often in a different currency, at a future date. Such instruments allowed money to be transferred across long distances without being physically moved, and because the exchange rate could conceal an element of interest, they also provided a way of lending at a time when the Church condemned usury.
By the early fourteenth century the fairs were in decline. Historians commonly point to the absorption of Champagne by the French crown, whose wars and heavy taxes disrupted trade, and to the opening of a regular sea route between Italy and Flanders. Yet the financial techniques developed there survived, passing to the Italian banking houses that would dominate European finance for the next two centuries.

Flaman kumaşının İtalya’yı fethi (‘Flemish Cloth’), Kilise’nin tefeciliğe karşı kampanyası (‘Campaign Against Usury’), deniz yolları (‘Sea Routes’) ve Fransız tacının savaşları (‘Wars’) metnin yalnızca küçük ayrıntılarıdır.

In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, a cycle of six fairs held in the county of Champagne, in north-eastern France, became the principal meeting point of European commerce. Merchants from Italy brought spices, silk and dyes obtained in the eastern Mediterranean, while traders from Flanders arrived with the woollen cloth for which their towns were famous. The fairs owed their success less to geography than to policy. The counts of Champagne guaranteed safe conduct to travelling merchants, levied moderate tolls and appointed special officials, the 'guards of the fairs', who enforced contracts and could pursue defaulting debtors even beyond the county's borders.
Perhaps the most lasting legacy of the fairs, however, was financial. Because each fair ended with a period devoted exclusively to settling accounts, merchants increasingly found it unnecessary to carry large sums of coin, which were heavy and vulnerable to theft. Instead, debts were recorded and offset against one another, and only the remaining balances were paid. Out of this practice grew the bill of exchange, a written order instructing an agent in another city to pay a specified sum, often in a different currency, at a future date. Such instruments allowed money to be transferred across long distances without being physically moved, and because the exchange rate could conceal an element of interest, they also provided a way of lending at a time when the Church condemned usury.
By the early fourteenth century the fairs were in decline. Historians commonly point to the absorption of Champagne by the French crown, whose wars and heavy taxes disrupted trade, and to the opening of a regular sea route between Italy and Flanders. Yet the financial techniques developed there survived, passing to the Italian banking houses that would dominate European finance for the next two centuries.

questions.passage:
Contact tracing, the process of identifying people who have been exposed to an infected person and monitoring or isolating them before they can pass the infection on, is among the oldest tools of public health. It was used against sexually transmitted infections in the first half of the twentieth century and played a central role in the eradication of smallpox, when teams sought out the contacts of every reported case and vaccinated them, creating a protective ring around each outbreak. Its appeal is easy to understand: by concentrating effort on those at highest risk, it promises to interrupt transmission without imposing restrictions on an entire population.
The effectiveness of the method, however, depends heavily on the characteristics of the disease. Smallpox was well suited to it because infected people generally became infectious only after symptoms appeared, and the distinctive rash made cases easy to recognise. Where a large proportion of transmission occurs before symptoms develop, or from people who never develop them at all, tracers are permanently one step behind: by the time a case is confirmed and its contacts are located, many of them may already have infected others. Speed therefore becomes decisive, and models suggest that even a delay of a few days can sharply reduce the number of infections prevented.
Practical and social obstacles add to these biological ones. Tracing requires a large trained workforce, rapid testing and, above all, the cooperation of the public. People who fear losing income, or who distrust the authorities, may be reluctant to name their contacts or to stay at home. Smartphone applications that record encounters between devices were widely promoted as a solution during recent epidemics, but their impact was limited by low uptake and by concerns about privacy. Contact tracing, in short, is a powerful instrument, but its success rests as much on public trust as on technical capacity.

Every day the Earth sweeps up tonnes of dust and small rocks from space, almost all of which burn up harmlessly in the atmosphere. Larger objects are far rarer, but their potential consequences are severe. An asteroid around twenty metres across exploded over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk in 2013, injuring more than a thousand people, mostly through broken glass, and an object roughly ten kilometres wide is widely believed to have contributed to the extinction of the dinosaurs. Although impacts of the latter kind occur only once in tens of millions of years, the scale of the possible damage has persuaded space agencies to take what is now called planetary defence seriously.
The first task is detection. Telescopic surveys have by now found the great majority of near-Earth asteroids larger than one kilometre, none of which appears to pose a significant threat in the coming century. Smaller objects, which are far more numerous and could still devastate a city, are much harder to spot, particularly those that approach from the direction of the Sun, where the sky cannot be observed at night. New survey telescopes, including one designed to operate in space and detect the heat these objects emit, are intended to close this gap.
Detection would be of limited value, however, without a means of responding. In 2022 a spacecraft was deliberately crashed into a small asteroid that orbits a larger companion, and subsequent observations showed that the collision had shortened its orbit by roughly half an hour, considerably more than many had predicted. The experiment demonstrated that a so-called kinetic impactor can alter an asteroid's path, provided that the object is discovered years in advance, since even a tiny change in velocity grows into a large shift in position over time. For this reason, experts insist that the most valuable resource in planetary defence is not force but warning time.

questions.passage:
In July 1944, while the Second World War was still being fought, delegates from forty-four Allied nations met at Bretton Woods in the United States to design a new international monetary order. Their thinking was shaped by the experience of the interwar years, when competitive devaluations, trade barriers and the breakdown of the gold standard had deepened the Great Depression. The system they created tied the currencies of member countries to the US dollar at fixed but adjustable rates, while the dollar itself was convertible into gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce. Two new institutions, the International Monetary Fund and what later became the World Bank, were established to lend to countries facing temporary difficulties and to finance reconstruction.
For roughly a quarter of a century the arrangement coincided with unprecedented growth in the advanced economies, though economists disagree about how much credit the system itself deserves for it. Its central weakness had been identified as early as 1960 by the economist Robert Triffin. Because the dollar served as the main reserve currency, the rest of the world could obtain the dollars it needed only if the United States ran persistent deficits; yet the larger those deficits grew, the less credible the American promise to exchange dollars for gold became. By the late 1960s, foreign holdings of dollars far exceeded American gold reserves, and confidence in the system began to erode.
In August 1971 President Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold, and by 1973 attempts to restore fixed rates had been abandoned. Most major currencies have floated against one another ever since. Nevertheless, the period left a lasting mark: the institutions founded at Bretton Woods still exist, and the dollar remains, by a wide margin, the world's dominant currency for trade and reserves.

the reasons why the Second World War was financed mainly by American loans

evidence that floating exchange rates have caused more crises than fixed ones

Altın standardının yeniden kurulmasını savunmak (‘should be restored’), savaşın Amerikan kredileriyle finansmanı (‘financed’), gelişmekte olan ülkelerle karşılaştırma (‘developing countries’) ve dalgalı kurların daha çok kriz yarattığı iddiası (‘more crises’) metinde yoktur.

In July 1944, while the Second World War was still being fought, delegates from forty-four Allied nations met at Bretton Woods in the United States to design a new international monetary order. Their thinking was shaped by the experience of the interwar years, when competitive devaluations, trade barriers and the breakdown of the gold standard had deepened the Great Depression. The system they created tied the currencies of member countries to the US dollar at fixed but adjustable rates, while the dollar itself was convertible into gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce. Two new institutions, the International Monetary Fund and what later became the World Bank, were established to lend to countries facing temporary difficulties and to finance reconstruction.
For roughly a quarter of a century the arrangement coincided with unprecedented growth in the advanced economies, though economists disagree about how much credit the system itself deserves for it. Its central weakness had been identified as early as 1960 by the economist Robert Triffin. Because the dollar served as the main reserve currency, the rest of the world could obtain the dollars it needed only if the United States ran persistent deficits; yet the larger those deficits grew, the less credible the American promise to exchange dollars for gold became. By the late 1960s, foreign holdings of dollars far exceeded American gold reserves, and confidence in the system began to erode.
In August 1971 President Nixon suspended the convertibility of the dollar into gold, and by 1973 attempts to restore fixed rates had been abandoned. Most major currencies have floated against one another ever since. Nevertheless, the period left a lasting mark: the institutions founded at Bretton Woods still exist, and the dollar remains, by a wide margin, the world's dominant currency for trade and reserves.
questions.text: It can be inferred from the passage that the problem identified by Triffin ----.
options: was solved when the World Bank began to finance reconstruction
made the system increasingly difficult to sustain as the world economy grew
was caused by the low price of gold in the interwar years
only affected countries that did not belong to the system
had no connection with the events of August 1971
questions.explanation: Triffin’e göre dünya ancak ABD açık verirse dolar bulabiliyordu, ama açıklar büyüdükçe altın vaadinin inandırıcılığı azalıyordu; dünya ekonomisi büyüyüp daha çok dolar gerektikçe sistemin sürdürülmesi zorlaşmıştır. Sorunun Dünya Bankası’yla çözüldüğü (‘was solved’), savaş arası altın fiyatından kaynaklandığı (‘low price of gold’), yalnızca üye olmayanları etkilediği (‘did not belong’) ve 1971 olaylarıyla bağlantısız olduğu (‘no connection’) çıkarımları metinle çelişir.

spread
stabilise
fluctuate

Gözlemevinin ne zamandır açık olduğu (‘How long’), teleskop tarihi üzerine bir kitap (‘book’) ve profesörün neden astronomiyi seçtiği (‘specialise’) soruları yanıtla ilgisizdir; gökyüzünün açık olacağını (‘clear’) varsayan soru ise bulut tahminiyle çelişir.

questions.passage:
Journalist: From next month, restaurants will have to display the calorie content of every dish on their menus.
Official: That's right, the regulation applies to all chains with more than twenty branches.

Does it actually change what people choose to eat?
Why do so many customers prefer fast food?

İlk zincirin ne zaman açıldığı (‘first restaurant chain’), bir yetişkinin günde kaç kalori alması gerektiği (‘consume’), geç saate kadar açık kalma (‘stay open’) ve fast food tercihinin nedeni (‘fast food’) soruları bu yanıta bağlanmaz.

questions.passage:
Visitor: Why are these old silver coins so irregular in shape?
Curator: They were cut and stamped by hand, and people often trimmed small amounts of metal from the edges.
Visitor: ----
Curator: Exactly. That's why later coins were given patterned edges, so that any trimming would be obvious at once.
Visitor: What a simple solution!
questions.text: Diyalogdaki boşluğa hangisi getirilmelidir?
options: Were coins also made of gold at that time?
How much would a coin like this be worth today?
Did the museum buy these coins at an auction?
Why didn't people simply use paper money instead?
So they could secretly profit from the silver they removed?
questions.explanation: Küratör ‘Exactly’ diyerek kenarları kesilen paralar için desenli kenar çözümünü anlatır; bu, insanların kestikleri gümüşten gizlice kazanç sağladığını doğrulatmak isteyen soruya uyar. Altın paraların da yapılıp yapılmadığı (‘gold’), bugünkü değeri (‘worth today’), müzenin paraları müzayededen alıp almadığı (‘auction’) ve kâğıt para (‘paper money’) soruları ‘Exactly’ yanıtıyla ve sonraki açıklamayla uyuşmaz.

questions.passage:

Yetişkinlerde yaygınlık (‘adults’), hastalığın belirtileri (‘symptoms’), aşının ilk ne zaman kullanıldığı (‘introduced’) ve okula gidip gidemeyeceği (‘school tomorrow’) soruları oranlarla verilen bu yanıta bağlanmaz.
